lessons.contracts__ijara:
In ijara, what is being sold is not the object itself but the right to make use of it — the benefit, so to speak. The object stays in the ownership of the one who is renting it out, and this single fact is the root from which everything else grows.

Because the object still belongs to the owner, he carries the risks that come with owning something. If the thing is destroyed through no fault of the person renting it — a fire, an accident, something beyond anyone's control — the loss falls on the owner, and the rental payments stop. Major repairs, insurance, the basic costs of ownership — these belong to him as well. The person renting is only responsible for ordinary upkeep, and for any damage caused by his own carelessness.

This is precisely what separates a genuine lease from a loan wearing the clothes of a lease. If the contract requires the renter to keep paying no matter what — even after the object itself is gone — then the risk was never truly resting with the owner. In that case, calling it a lease does not make it one.

There is a form called ijara muntahia bittamlik — a lease that ends with the property passing to the person who rented it. It is used in place of a mortgage or a car loan. Scholars insist on one condition: the transfer of ownership must be arranged as a separate promise, a gift or a sale set apart from the lease itself. It must not be woven into the lease in a way that turns the rental payments into disguised installments. If the two are merged, what you end up with is really a sale on credit, simply wearing the name of a lease.

Charging a percentage as a penalty for late payment is not permitted in ijara, for the same reason it is not permitted in murabaha.

And there is something here worth remembering by anyone who has ever hired a person to do work, not only equipment to use. It is reported that on the Day of Judgment, the Prophet ﷺ will stand against three kinds of people, and among them is the one who hired a worker, received his full work, and did not give him his wage. Ijara is not only about renting things — it is also about the trust placed in someone's labor, and what is owed to them for it.
lessons.contracts__mudaraba-musharaka:
When money is placed in someone else's business, there are really only two honest arrangements, and both of them tie the profit to genuine risk. That is what separates them from interest, and it is worth understanding clearly, especially if you are thinking about where to place savings you have built up over many years.

The first is called mudaraba. One side provides the capital — this could be you, placing savings into a venture. The other side, the manager, provides the work and the expertise. The profit is split according to a ratio agreed in advance, say sixty to forty. But here is the heart of it: if the venture loses money, it is the owner of the capital who bears that loss, while the manager loses only his time and effort and walks away with nothing for it. The exception is if the loss happened because the manager was careless or broke the agreed terms — then responsibility shifts to him.

The second is mushataka, a fuller partnership. Here both sides put in capital, and both may also take part in running the business. The profit can be divided by agreement in whatever way the partners settle on — the one who also does the work can rightly take a larger share, even beyond what his capital alone would suggest. But losses are different: they must always be shared strictly in proportion to how much each person put in. This is not something the partners are free to renegotiate.

There is one rule that decides whether an arrangement is truly a partnership or only interest wearing a different name: a share of the profit may be agreed upon, but a fixed sum may never be guaranteed to either side regardless of outcome. The moment someone is promised a set amount no matter what happens, the risk has vanished, and what remains is a loan carrying interest, whatever it may be called. For the same reason, one partner cannot promise the other that his original capital will simply be returned to him untouched.

There is a form of this partnership that may be especially relevant if you are thinking about property — for yourself or as part of arranging things for your family. It is called diminishing partnership. A financing party and a client buy a home together, perhaps in a split such as twenty to eighty. The client lives in the home and pays rent for the portion still owned by the financing party, while at the same time gradually buying out that portion. As the client's share grows, the financing party's share shrinks, and the rent shrinks along with it, until eventually the whole property belongs to the client. This is one of the main ways offered within Islamic finance as an alternative to a conventional mortgage.

There is also something said about partnership that gives it a particular weight. It is related that Allah says He is a third partner with two people in business, so long as neither betrays the other — and that as soon as betrayal enters, He withdraws from them. It is a reminder that this kind of dealing is not only a financial matter, but one of trust between people, watched over.
lessons.contracts__murabaha:
Murabaha is the most common contract in Islamic finance, and also the one most often misunderstood or wrongly copied. It is worth understanding properly, because you may come across it when a bank or financier offers to help you purchase something — a car, equipment, household goods — instead of simply lending you money.

The idea itself is simple. Rather than giving you money and charging you interest on it, the financier buys the item you need. He becomes its actual owner. Then he sells it to you at a price he states openly — the original cost plus a profit margin, named clearly. You then pay this agreed price in instalments.

For this arrangement to genuinely be murabaha, and not something wearing its name, three conditions must hold.

The first is real ownership. The financier must actually purchase the item and carry the risk of owning it before he sells it on to you. If something happened to the goods between his purchase and your purchase — damage, loss — that loss would be his, not yours. Without this, the whole arrangement collapses into selling something one does not actually possess.

The second is an openly stated profit. What makes murabaha different from an ordinary sale is precisely that the cost and the margin are both named plainly, not hidden inside a single price. If the margin is concealed, the contract no longer qualifies as murabaha.

The third is a fixed price. The total amount is set once, at the start, and does not grow because payment is late. If the amount increases with time, interest has returned in substance, whatever the contract is called.

It is worth being honest about a real criticism raised within the industry itself. If the financier's ownership lasts only minutes and exists only on paper, the economic result looks no different from an interest-bearing loan. Some scholars say this plainly, and it is a fair point. This is exactly why industry standards spend so much effort spelling out what counts as genuine ownership rather than a formality. Whether everyday practice truly lives up to these standards is a continuing, honest debate within the field — not something this lesson can settle for you.

A practical question for anyone your age managing savings and thinking ahead: what happens if a payment is late, given that the price cannot simply be increased afterward? The accepted practice is that a fixed penalty may be agreed in advance, but it cannot become income for the financier — it is directed to charity instead. This keeps a real incentive to pay on time without turning someone's hardship into profit for another. And it is worth remembering that the Quran itself instructs that a debtor in genuine difficulty should be given more time, not pressured further.
lessons.contracts__salam-istisna:
There is a well-known general rule in Islamic dealings: you cannot sell something you do not actually have. It sounds simple, but real life has always needed some careful exceptions to this — not to break the rule, but because there are genuine situations where a producer or maker needs support before the goods even exist. Two such arrangements have long been recognised, and it is worth understanding both, since they may come up if you ever think about how family money is placed, lent, or used to help someone starting a venture.

The first is called salam. Here the buyer pays the full price immediately, and the seller commits to deliver the goods later, at an agreed time. This is not left vague — the conditions are stated plainly: payment upfront is only valid when the quantity, the weight, and the time of delivery are all clearly known. The goods themselves must be something that can be described by type and quality — a certain grade of wheat, for example — not a one-of-a-kind item that has no equivalent. And the buyer must pay the entire sum at once, right away; paying only part now and part later is not allowed, since that would turn into one debt being exchanged for another, which is not permitted.

Think of why this exists. A farmer needs money in spring, to buy seed and prepare the land, but the harvest will not come until autumn. Salam lets him receive funds now without borrowing at interest. The buyer, in turn, usually pays somewhat less than what the market price is expected to be later — but takes on real risk in exchange: the harvest might fail, or the price might fall by the time it is ready. The risk is shared honestly between both sides, rather than placed entirely on the one with less power in the arrangement.

The second is istisna. This applies when someone commissions something to be made — a house, a boat, machinery, a batch of equipment — something that does not yet exist and will be built to specification. It differs from salam in two ways. Payment does not need to be made all at once; it can be made in stages, as the work progresses. And the timing is far more flexible — what matters most is that the item and its specifications are described with precision.

This is why istisna is commonly used in construction and larger projects: the client pays according to the stages of the work, the builder produces according to an agreed specification, and both sides are genuinely engaged in real production — not simply trading one debt for another.

What both arrangements share is this: the item being made or delivered must be described so precisely that if a disagreement ever arose about whether it matched what was promised, the matter could be settled clearly. This precision of description is exactly what removes the uncertainty that Islamic dealings are careful to avoid.
lessons.contracts__why-contract:
The word "Islamic" printed on a brochure or a bank product tells you nothing by itself. What matters is how the agreement is actually built, and that can be checked with one question: who carries the risk.

Three things are forbidden, and nearly every practical rule you will meet comes from these three. Riba is profit taken without risk, simply because money was lent. Gharar is excessive uncertainty — the thing being sold, its price, or its timing is not properly known, so one side is essentially buying blind. Maysir is gambling on an outcome, where what one person wins, the other must lose.

From these three prohibitions come rules you can actually use.

You cannot sell what you do not own. Whoever sells something must genuinely possess it and bear the risk of owning it — if the item is lost or destroyed before it changes hands, the loss falls on the seller, not the buyer. This is exactly why properly structured Islamic financing works through the actual purchase and sale of real property, rather than simply handing over money and charging for its use.

The thing being sold and its price must be clearly known. There is a verse in the Quran about writing down a debt that is the longest verse in the entire Book, and its whole purpose is to make sure an obligation is put in writing, witnessed, and given a fixed term. Uncertainty in a contract is not treated as a small detail to overlook — removing it is the subject of its own instruction.

Honesty matters more than the profit at stake. A hadith tells us that both sides of a transaction have the right to walk away from it until they part ways; if they were honest and explained things clearly, their sale is blessed, but if they lied and concealed something, whatever blessing was in that sale is destroyed.

Whatever conditions the two sides agreed to must be honoured. If something was written into the agreement, it is binding, and both sides are expected to carry it out.

This gives you a simple way to look at any financial product placed in front of you — including ones with an appealing name, or ones a relative recommends because "everyone says it is halal." Do not start by asking what it is called. Ask what exactly is being sold, who owned it and at which moment, and who would bear the loss if it were destroyed. The answers to those three questions tell you far more than any label ever could.
lessons.halal-income__crypto:
Whether cryptocurrency itself is permissible property is not something this lesson can settle for you — scholars who have studied the question carefully have reached different conclusions, and the disagreement is real, not a matter of small detail.

Those who permit it reason this way: in Islamic law, wealth (mal) is anything that people recognise as having value and find useful. A digital asset that people accept and exchange for goods or services fits that description, and buying or selling it for immediate payment is, in their view, not fundamentally different from exchanging one currency for another.

Those who forbid it reason differently: the asset has no backing and no production behind it, its price moves purely with market mood, and that kind of extreme uncertainty is exactly what is meant by gharar — the excessive ambiguity the Prophet ﷺ forbade in a transaction. They add that most trading in it is speculation rather than genuine use, which brings in maysir, the element of gambling.

There is a middle position, and it may be the most useful one for someone trying to manage their own money honestly: separate the question of what the asset is from the question of what you do with it. The debate about its nature can continue among scholars, but a number of common practices around cryptocurrency fall under well-established prohibitions no matter how that debate is eventually resolved.

Here is what can be said with confidence, without taking a side in the larger dispute:

- A fixed return promised in advance for lending out your funds — sometimes offered as a guaranteed yearly percentage — is riba, an increase taken simply for the use of money over time. This is true whatever the underlying asset is.
- Trading on borrowed money, or through contracts that bet on a future price without any real exchange taking place, carries both gharar and maysir. You are wagering on an outcome, not taking part in genuine trade.
- A project whose actual business is gambling, indecency, or interest-based lending is excluded for that reason alone, exactly as an ordinary company would be.
- If you hold cryptocurrency as savings, and you follow the scholarly opinion that treats it as wealth, it is included in your zakat calculation at its market value on the date you calculate — the same way gold, savings, or any other form of wealth would be assessed.

This also explains a choice we have made at AM Network. We have deliberately chosen not to issue our own tradable coin, even though doing so is the easiest way to raise money for a project like ours. The reason is precisely the gharar and maysir involved: when a coin's value depends only on what people expect it to become, that value is undefined, and whatever one holder gains tends to come out of another holder's pocket. Instead, our income is structured as ujrah — a clearly stated fee for a service we actually provide, between one and two and a half percent of each transaction. We use the underlying digital ledger only as a record that anyone can check, not as a means of creating an asset to sell.

One thing is worth saying plainly. If you already hold cryptocurrency, or are thinking about whether to, this is a matter to raise with someone qualified to advise you personally, not something to settle from an article. What this lesson can do is show you where the boundaries are certain. The question of what the asset itself is, we cannot answer for you.
lessons.halal-income__halal-basics:
Whether income is halal is not decided by the amount involved, nor by how respectable the position or profession sounds. It comes down to three things: what is being sold, how the money was obtained, and on what terms the agreement was made.

The first is the subject of the sale itself. If the goods or service are forbidden in themselves, no amount of honesty or fairness in carrying out the transaction changes that. Trading in intoxicants, gambling, or spreading indecency remain forbidden no matter how carefully or courteously the business is run.

The second is the manner in which the money changes hands. The Quran forbids consuming one another's wealth wrongfully, making an exception for trade conducted by mutual consent. Cheating on weight, hiding a defect from a buyer, taking what belongs to someone else, or paying and receiving a bribe — all of these make the money gained forbidden, even when the item being sold is perfectly permissible on its own.

The third is the contract itself. Even a permissible good can be sold in a forbidden way — through interest, through excessive uncertainty about what is actually being exchanged, or through terms where one party's gain is directly built on the other party's loss.

Between what is clearly permitted and what is clearly forbidden lies an area of things that are unclear. The Prophet ﷺ said that the permissible is clear and the forbidden is clear, and between the two lie doubtful matters that many people do not know how to judge; whoever avoids the doubtful has protected his faith and his honour. This is not a call to suspicion over every little thing. It is a simple rule for moments of genuine uncertainty: find out first, and until you know, do not rush ahead.

This matters beyond questions of bookkeeping. In one hadith, a man is described travelling far from home, dishevelled and covered in dust, raising his hands to the sky and calling out — yet his food is forbidden, his drink is forbidden, his clothing is forbidden, and he has been nourished on what is forbidden. The question is then asked: how, then, could he expect to be answered? The source of one's earnings touches more than the wallet.

And there is a warning that sounds remarkably current: a time will come when a person will no longer care whether the wealth he takes comes from what is permitted or from what is forbidden. Paying attention to the source is exactly what is asked of us — a fitting thing to keep in mind when reviewing savings gathered over many years, or thinking through how they should be passed on.
lessons.halal-income__savings-takaful:
Commercial insurance troubles scholars for three reasons at once, and it is worth understanding all three, because together they explain why the alternative was built so differently.

The first is uncertainty about the outcome itself. You pay a fixed sum for a result that is entirely unknown — you might pay premiums for twenty years and receive nothing back, or pay a single instalment and receive a large payout. The second is that the whole arrangement depends on chance: one side's gain is the other side's loss, much like a wager. The third is that the reserves collected from policyholders are typically invested by the insurer at interest, which brings in a further problem regardless of the first two.

Takaful was built to avoid all three, and the difference is not a matter of naming — it is a matter of who actually owns the money. In takaful, participants place their contributions into a shared fund as a form of mutual help, not as payment for a service. Losses suffered by any participant are covered from this common fund. The company that runs the scheme does not own the fund at all — it manages it, and is paid either an agreed fee for that management, or a share of the profit earned when the fund's money is invested. If the fund shows a surplus at the end of the period, that surplus goes back to the participants, or is carried forward for them — it does not become the operator's profit.

So the essential difference is this: in commercial insurance, you and the insurer are two sides of a deal with opposing interests. In takaful, you and the other participants are on the same side, helping one another, and the company is simply a hired manager of that mutual arrangement. This mirrors a broader principle familiar to us — helping one another in good and in mindfulness of God.

It is worth being honest about where takaful stands. It is not something handed down directly in the texts — it is a structure that scholars worked out in the twentieth century to meet a real need. Different companies implement it differently, some more faithfully to the principle than others, so if you are considering a takaful product, the actual contract deserves a careful look rather than trust in the label alone.

A separate matter is insurance required by law — such as vehicle insurance or certain medical cover that a country makes compulsory. Scholars discuss this under the principle of necessity, and many do not consider a person at fault for carrying something the law obliges and that cannot reasonably be avoided.

On savings, briefly: what is permitted includes a current account that carries no interest, an account structured on profit-sharing rather than fixed interest, physical gold and silver, and a genuine share in a real business. What is not permitted is an interest-bearing deposit, whatever name the bank gives it. And one thing worth keeping in mind for your own planning: savings held in any of the permitted forms are still included when calculating zakat.

If a particular savings product or a specific takaful contract you are looking at is not covered clearly by what is above, this lesson does not go further into it — that is a good question to bring to the tutor or to a qualified scholar who can look at the actual terms.
lessons.halal-income__screening:
When you buy a share, you are not buying a piece of paper — you are buying a portion of an actual business, with all that this business does. Because of this, checking a share properly means looking at it on two levels, one after the other.

The first level is simple: what does the company actually do? If its main business is something forbidden — making or selling alcohol, pork, tobacco, gambling and lotteries, indecent entertainment, or if it is itself an interest-based bank or a commercial insurance company — then the matter is settled at once. Such companies are set aside regardless of anything else, because their earnings by their very nature rest on riba.

The second level is financial, and it is more delicate. Almost every large company today keeps some money in interest-bearing accounts or carries some interest-based debt. Finding a company that is entirely free of this is rare. Because of this reality, modern scholars working on this question have set acceptable limits, so that ordinary people are not left with no way to invest at all. One such standard, known as AAOIFI Standard No. 21, allows a company through if three conditions hold: interest-based debt stays below thirty percent of the company's market value, interest-based deposits and investments stay below thirty percent as well, and income from forbidden activities stays below five percent of total income.

Two honest points need to be said here, plainly. First, these percentages come from a modern industry standard set by qualified scholars — they are not a verse or a hadith, and they were never meant to be treated as such. Second, different reputable bodies calculate this differently. Some measure against market value, others against total assets, and the thresholds they use are not always identical. This means the same company might pass under one standard and fail under another. That is not a mistake on anyone's part — it simply reflects that sincere scholars have approached the same difficult question with different careful methods.

There is also the matter of purification. If a company you hold shares in has a small portion of forbidden income within these permitted limits, then that same small portion of your dividends or profit is not rightfully yours to keep for yourself. It should be calculated and given away for the general good — not as an act of charity for which you hope reward, but simply as a cleansing of your wealth from what does not belong to it.

One more practical matter, especially relevant if you hold shares as part of your savings. Shares you own do count toward zakat, but scholars distinguish two situations. If you bought shares meaning to sell them again for profit, they are counted at their full market value. If you are holding them for the dividends they bring, many scholars hold that only the portion corresponding to the company's current, liquid assets — the share of that belonging to your own holding — needs to be counted. This lesson does not go further into how that calculation is worked out step by step; for the exact figures in your own case, it would be right to ask your tutor or a qualified scholar directly.
lessons.riba__riba-today:
The sign to watch for is always the same: does the extra money come from time — from simply waiting — rather than from goods, work, or a shared risk. Once you learn to notice that, it becomes easier to recognise riba in the ordinary financial matters that come up in life, including in retirement.

Take a credit card. Owning the card itself is not riba. Riba appears only when interest is charged on a balance that was not paid off. If someone pays the full amount within the interest-free period, no interest is charged, and so this particular riba does not occur. There remains a separate question — about the contract itself, which allows for such interest even if it is never actually charged — and scholars differ on how to view that. This lesson does not settle that part; if it matters to you, it is worth asking a knowledgeable scholar directly.

A personal loan or a car loan taken with interest is a plainer case: you return more than you borrowed, and the difference is simply payment for time. The same applies, from the other side, to an interest-bearing savings deposit. When you place money in such an account, it becomes a debt the bank owes you, and the interest added to it is an increase on that debt — the same riba, just received rather than paid.

Instalment payments need to be looked at more carefully, since they can go either way. If a seller sets one fixed price for an item bought in instalments — even if that price is higher than the cash price — and the amount is agreed once and does not change afterward, most scholars consider this a legitimate sale: a price was set for goods with delayed payment, nothing more. But if the amount grows because a payment is late, or if interest is added onto the remaining balance, that becomes riba.

On housing loans: an ordinary interest-bearing mortgage falls under the prohibition of riba. There is a recognised difference of opinion, however, about the position of Muslims living in places where an Islamic alternative is not available — some scholars permit it in cases of real necessity, when there is truly no other option, while others do not. This is not something to decide on the basis of an article. If you are weighing a housing loan, bring your actual situation to a scholar who can hear the details and advise you properly.

As for late-payment penalties: if the penalty is calculated as a percentage and grows the longer the debt goes unpaid, that is riba. A fixed one-time charge meant to cover actual administrative cost is judged differently by scholars.
lessons.riba__two-kinds:
Scholars distinguish two kinds of riba, and it helps to keep them apart, because they arise in quite different situations.

The first kind is the riba of debt. This is what most people simply call usury: an addition charged for the use of someone else's money, or for delaying a payment. It covers interest on a loan, interest that accumulates on an unpaid card balance, income from an interest-bearing deposit, and also penalty interest that grows for every day a payment is late. For someone who has spent a lifetime being careful with money, this is probably the familiar face of riba — the one most people already recognise and try to avoid.

The second kind is the riba of exchange, and it is less often talked about, though it matters a great deal for anyone holding gold or jewellery accumulated over the years. This riba appears when things of the same kind are exchanged in unequal amounts, or with a delay. A well-known hadith names six such things: gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, and salt. The rule set down for them is this: if you exchange one for the other of the very same kind, it must be equal amount for equal amount, and handed over on the spot. So ten grams of gold cannot be exchanged for twelve grams of gold, even if the twelve grams are of lower quality or older workmanship. The correct way is to sell the gold for money, and then use that money to buy the other gold separately.

A practical consequence of this second kind, easy to overlook, concerns exchanging currencies. Changing one currency for another is allowed, at the going rate, but the exchange must be settled immediately — both sides receiving what is due to them within the same transaction. If the settlement is delayed when money is being exchanged for money, that delay itself introduces riba.

This second kind can feel distant from everyday concerns, yet it is precisely what explains why Islamic financial institutions structure their dealings around buying and selling an actual good, rather than simply lending money and charging for its use.
lessons.riba__way-out:
Finding out that some part of your savings or dealings has been touched by riba is not a verdict against you. It is simply the point where the way out begins. The Quran speaks directly to people in exactly this position: leave what remains of the interest — meaning, stop what is still ongoing. There is no call here to despair over years already passed. The instruction is forward-looking.

The first step is to stop anything new from starting. No new interest-bearing agreements, no new cards that add interest charges, no new deposits placed for the sake of interest return. Until the inflow is stopped, trying to undo the past does very little good — it is like bailing water while the tap is still running.

The second step is to see the whole picture clearly. Write it down: where each obligation is, how much, at what rate, and for how long. Many people who have lived with this for years genuinely do not know the exact total. It is often this uncertainty itself, more than the debt, that keeps a person from beginning.

The third step is a matter of plain arithmetic: pay down whatever carries the highest rate first. The higher the rate, the faster it grows, and the longer it is left, the more interest ends up being paid in the end.

The fourth matter concerns interest that has already been received — for instance, amounts added to a savings deposit over the years. Scholars broadly agree that this should not be kept and spent on oneself. The common view is that it should be given away for the general good, without seeking any reward for it, since this is a cleansing of one's wealth rather than an act of charity. The exact method of doing this is best confirmed with someone knowledgeable, since particular situations can differ.

The fifth step is not to carry this alone. People arrive at this point from very different paths — a mortgage taken years ago, an inheritance that came with existing arrangements, a business with some interest-based financing folded into it. A general rule cannot substitute for someone examining your actual situation. It is worth seeking out a scholar who can sit with the details of your case specifically.

Last, it is worth saying plainly: shame and worry are what cause people to put off this conversation for years, while the debt itself keeps growing in the meantime. A decision made early and honestly is always lighter to carry than one made late.
lessons.riba__what-is-riba:
Riba is an increase agreed upon in advance, received not for work done, not for risk taken, not for goods provided, but simply for the fact that money was lent, or because one thing was exchanged for an unequal amount of its own kind.

Picture something you may well have encountered in your own dealings over the years: you lend someone a sum, say a thousand, and you ask for eleven hundred back. That extra hundred is riba. It makes no difference what name is put on it — interest, a service charge, a fee for the delay in repayment. What matters is where the increase comes from. It comes purely from the debt itself, not from any trade, not from any shared venture.

Why the prohibition is so firm. The Quran sets riba directly against trade. In trade, the seller carries real risk — the goods might not sell, might spoil, might lose value before they are sold. In riba there is no such risk: the lender receives the agreed increase regardless of what happens to the borrower, even if the borrower has lost everything. A gain with no risk attached places the whole burden on the weaker side, and over time wealth moves away from those in need and toward those who already have plenty.

The responsibility here is not limited to the one who collects the increase. A hadith names five people together: the one who takes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes the contract down, and the two witnesses to it — and says they are all alike in this matter. Being part of arranging an interest-based agreement, even without taking any profit yourself, falls under the same warning.

It is worth being precise about what is actually forbidden. It is the increase taken simply for a debt. Profit earned through honest trade, through renting something out, through a joint investment where both sides share the risk — this is permitted, and indeed encouraged. The concern here is not profit itself. It is profit taken without risk, at the expense of someone else's need — something worth keeping in mind as you think through savings held over many years, or how an estate might be arranged for those who come after you.
lessons.zakat-basics__eight-categories:
The people who may receive zakat are not left to personal judgement or custom. The Quran names them directly — eight categories, stated plainly, and this is not a set of examples to draw inspiration from. The circle is closed. Zakat goes to these, and not, properly speaking, to anyone outside them.

The eight are:

- The poor, whose means fall short of covering basic needs.
- The destitute, whose situation is even more severe than the poor's.
- Those who work in collecting and distributing zakat — their labour is paid for out of the zakat itself.
- Those whose hearts are to be reconciled — this includes people newly come to Islam who find themselves in a difficult position.
- Those held in bondage, to free them — historically this meant ransoming slaves and captives; scholars today extend this to freeing people from servitude and exploitation.
- Those burdened with debts they cannot repay.
- In the cause of God — a category scholars have understood with varying degrees of breadth.
- The traveller stranded without means, even if he is a person of substance back home.

Just as important is who does not receive zakat. You do not give it to those you are already responsible for supporting — parents, children, a spouse. Their upkeep is your duty regardless, and zakat cannot be used to discharge an obligation you already carry. Nor does it go to someone who is comfortably well off and does not fit any of the eight categories above. And most scholars hold that it should not go to the descendants of the Prophet, peace be upon him, the family of Banu Hashim, for whom zakat is not permitted.

This is worth pausing on, given a lifetime of family ties, because there is good news within the restriction. A brother, a sister, an uncle, a nephew or niece — anyone you are not already obligated to support — can rightly receive your zakat if they are in need. In fact, scholars consider this better than giving to a stranger, because it joins the act of zakat to the maintaining of family bonds, which carries its own weight in this faith.

This is also the standard AM Network works from. When the system evaluates who may receive support, it is measuring a person's situation against this same list from the Quran — nothing broader, nothing narrower. And the confirmation that someone truly exists and truly is in need is never left to the system alone; it comes from a real person on the ground — an imam, a volunteer, someone from a partner organisation who can vouch for the case directly.
lessons.zakat-basics__nisab:
Nisab is the threshold that decides whether zakat applies to you at all. If what you own falls below this line, nothing is due — not a partial amount, not a token sum. Nothing. This exists so that zakat is taken only from genuine surplus, from those who have more than they need, not from someone quietly managing on modest savings or a pension.

The threshold itself is fixed in two metals: eighty-five grams of gold, or five hundred ninety-five grams of silver. In practice, this is translated into your own currency using the current market price of the metal — which is why the exact figure changes from year to year, and why it's worth checking again each time rather than relying on a number from a previous year.

Here scholars differ, and it's worth understanding why. Gold and silver give noticeably different thresholds — the silver-based one is, in today's market, considerably lower than the gold-based one. Some scholars calculate using gold, others using silver. Many contemporary scholars and charitable funds prefer the silver threshold precisely because it is lower: more people end up qualifying to pay, and more support reaches those who need it. This is a recognised, respected difference of opinion — not a matter of one side being correct and the other mistaken. If you're unsure which to follow, this is a good question to bring to a knowledgeable teacher who can guide you based on your own circumstances.

For someone your age, with gold and jewellery gathered over many years, this distinction matters. A ring or a set of bangles kept since a wedding decades ago, savings built up slowly, a pension held in an account — all of this is measured against whichever threshold you follow, and only the portion above it is ever relevant to zakat.

The second condition is time: your wealth must remain at or above the nisab for one full lunar year, roughly three hundred fifty-four days. The clock starts the day your holdings first reach the threshold. If the amount dips below nisab at some point during the year but rises above it again by year's end, most scholars hold that the year still counts — what matters is where you stood at the beginning and where you stand at the end, not every fluctuation in between.

In practice, the simplest approach is to choose one date on the lunar calendar and check your wealth against it every year, without fail. Many people choose Ramadan, simply because it's easier to remember and naturally brings the matter to mind each year. For someone thinking about keeping their affairs settled and clear for the future, having one fixed date you return to each year — rather than calculating anew each time — brings a real sense of order to this.

If any part of your own situation isn't addressed clearly here — inherited gold, jointly held savings, or anything more particular — this lesson doesn't go into that level of detail, and it would be worth asking your tutor or a qualified scholar directly.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-counts:
Zakat is due on wealth that grows or that simply sits and accumulates. It is not due on things you use in daily life. The line between these two is worth understanding clearly, because after a lifetime of working and saving, most people have both kinds mixed together.

What is counted for zakat:

- Cash in hand, money in bank accounts and savings, whatever form it takes.
- Gold and silver in any form — bars, coins, and jewellery alike.
- Goods bought with the intention of resale, valued at what they are worth today, not what you originally paid for them.
- Investments — shares, business shares, digital assets.
- Money owed to you, if you genuinely expect it to be repaid.

What is not counted:

- The home you live in, and the ordinary things inside it — clothing, furniture, dishes.
- The car you use for yourself.
- The tools of your own work — a craftsman's equipment, a computer someone uses for their trade, a taxi driver's car.
- A business's building and equipment. Only the goods held for sale are counted, not the shop or workshop that holds them.

If you have debts you are obligated to pay, these are subtracted from the total before working out zakat — most scholars say this applies especially to debts that are already due.

There is one point where the scholars have long differed, and it concerns jewellery worn for personal use rather than kept as savings. The Hanafi school holds that zakat is due on gold and silver jewellery regardless of whether it is worn or stored. A number of scholars from other schools hold that if the jewellery is worn in reasonable amounts, and not simply kept as a store of wealth, no zakat is due on it. This is an old and recognised difference of opinion, not a matter of one side being simply right or wrong. It would be worth raising with someone knowledgeable to decide which view to follow for your own situation, especially if jewellery makes up a meaningful part of what you hold.

Whatever the total comes to, once debts are subtracted, the rate is the same for everything: two and a half percent, that is, one part in forty.

If any part of your situation is not addressed here — for instance, how this applies to inheritance you have not yet distributed — this lesson does not cover it, and it is best to raise it directly with the tutor or a qualified scholar.
lessons.zakat-basics__what-is-zakat:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam — an obligation upon every Muslim whose wealth has reached a certain threshold. It is not a voluntary act of kindness, and it is not a gift handed down to someone poorer. It is a right that the needy hold over the wealth of the well-off, a right established by Allah Himself.

The word "zakat" carries two meanings at once: purification and growth. When a person pays it, two things happen together — the wealth that remains is purified, and the heart is purified of stinginess and of too tight a grip on what one owns.

It helps to understand clearly how zakat differs from sadaqah, ordinary charity. Zakat is obligatory. It has an exact rate — 2.5% of accumulated wealth — along with firm conditions and a defined circle of recipients laid out in the Quran. Sadaqah, by contrast, is voluntary, has no fixed amount, and can be given to anyone, at any time, for any reason that moves the heart. Failing to pay zakat when it is due is a sin. Failing to give sadaqah is not.

There is one point worth sitting with carefully, especially for someone who has spent a lifetime building up savings, gold, or jewellery: zakat is not taken from income. It is taken from what has accumulated and remained with a person over time. It is not calculated the moment a pension arrives or a payment is received. It applies to what is left sitting, untouched, once a full year has passed. A person may receive a good deal over the course of a year, but if it is all spent and nothing remains above the threshold by year's end, no zakat is owed on it. What matters is what stays, not what passes through one's hands.

This distinction matters greatly for someone thinking about gold kept over many years, or savings set aside for children and grandchildren. The question is never "how much came in this year," but "what remains, untouched, once the year has turned." This lesson does not go into how that threshold is calculated for gold, jewellery, or mixed savings — that is a matter with real detail to it, and it is best raised directly with the tutor or a qualified scholar so it can be applied properly to one's own situation.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__sadaqah:
When people hear the word "садака," they often think first of money — a note handed to someone in need, a sum given to a mosque or a cause. That is садака, certainly, but it is far from the whole of it. There is a hadith that says every joint in a person's body owes a садака each day the sun rises, and then it lists what fulfils that: judging fairly between two people, helping someone with their mount or their load, a kind word, every step taken toward prayer, removing something harmful from the road. None of this requires a coin. A person with an empty pocket is not a person without means to give.

This matters at any stage of life, but perhaps especially once the pace of earning has slowed and a person may feel their giving is now limited to what savings allow. It isn't. A fair word to a grandchild, patience with a neighbour, walking to pray rather than driving — all of it counts.

On the question of increase, the Quran gives an image rather than a formula: someone who spends their wealth in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears, and in every ear a hundred grains. It is a picture of multiplication, not a guaranteed arithmetic — but the direction is clear.

There is also a warning worth holding onto, stated just as plainly: do not spoil your acts of charity with reminders of your generosity or with hurtful words. If you give something and later bring it up to make the recipient feel small, or remind them of what they owe you, the Quran says this destroys the very giving itself. It is placed next to giving only to be seen — that is how seriously it is treated.

This is part of why quiet giving is preferred. Giving openly has its place — it can encourage others to give as well. But to give quietly, especially to someone poor, is described as better. Quiet giving protects the dignity of the person receiving, and it protects the sincerity of the person giving.

Then there is садака джария — giving that keeps working after the person who gave it has died. A hadith explains that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing садака, knowledge that continues to be used by others, and a righteous child who prays for them.

For someone thinking about savings gathered over many years, gold set aside, or how things will be arranged after they are gone, this idea changes how giving can be thought about. A one-time gift meets today's need and then it is finished. But something that keeps functioning — a well, a book, someone taught a skill, a tool still in use — keeps giving on its own, without needing you there. This is exactly the thinking behind вакф, which the next lesson takes up.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__three-forms:
Over a lifetime, most people accumulate three kinds of relationship with their wealth, and it helps to see clearly how they differ — especially now, when questions of savings, gold set aside for years, and what to leave behind become more pressing.

The first is zakat. This is not optional. If your savings or gold have sat with you for a full lunar year and exceed the threshold, 2.5% of that amount is owed. It is not owed to whomever you choose — the Quran names eight categories of people who may receive it, and that circle cannot be widened or substituted by personal preference. Once given, the wealth belongs fully and finally to the recipient.

The second is sadaqah — voluntary giving. Here there is no fixed amount, no waiting period, and no restriction on who may receive it. Many hadith make clear that sadaqah is not only money — a kind word or a small act of help counts too. Like zakat, once given, it is gone from your hand for good.

The third is waqf, and it works differently from the other two. With waqf, the thing itself — a piece of land, a building, a fund — is taken out of circulation permanently. It cannot be sold, gifted, or passed down as inheritance. What gets distributed is only what it produces: the crop, the rent, the income. If you place a house into waqf, you have not given away the house — you have given away all its future benefit, without end. This is worth sitting with for anyone thinking about how to arrange their affairs for the years ahead.

Now, the rule most often misunderstood: sadaqah does not stand in for zakat. You could give away, over a year, ten times the value of your zakat obligation in voluntary charity, and still owe zakat in full — if it was never set aside and paid with the specific intention of zakat, to someone from the eight named categories. What is obligatory is not settled by what is voluntary, no matter how generous the voluntary giving has been.

The reverse is equally true: zakat is a floor, not a ceiling. It marks the minimum owed, not the limit of what generosity can be. The Quran says that true righteousness is not reached until a person gives from what he loves — and this speaks precisely to sadaqah, to what is given beyond duty, from what is dear to the heart, not merely from what is easy to spare.

And there is one more thing set directly against this whole picture: usury and charity move in opposite directions. The Quran says that Allah erases the increase gained through usury and multiplies what is given in charity. Two movements of wealth, pulling apart from one another — one that shrinks what looks like gain, and one that grows what looks like loss.
lessons.zakat-sadaqah-waqf__waqf:
The idea of вакф began with a very ordinary question. Умар ибн аль-Хаттаб came into possession of land in Хайбар — the best property he owned — and he did not know what to do with it. He asked, and he was told: if you wish, keep the land itself untouched, and give away what it produces. Умар did exactly that. He set it down as a condition that the land itself could never be sold, never given away as a gift, never passed on through inheritance — but what it yielded, season after season, would go to the poor, to relatives, to freeing people from bondage, and to travellers.

That one arrangement contains the whole idea. There is a body — the asset itself — and there is the fruit it produces. The body is frozen permanently. It cannot be sold, cannot be inherited, cannot change hands. The fruit — the rent, the harvest, the income — is what gets distributed, according to the purpose its founder named.

Out of this simple structure grew wells that gave water to travellers, hospitals that treated the sick without charge, libraries, shelters for those on a journey, even universities that carried on for centuries. These were not one-time acts of charity. They were institutions that kept working, supporting themselves indefinitely from what they produced.

The conditions a founder sets down are not just words of good intention — they are binding. There is a settled principle that Muslims are bound by the conditions they set. If someone specifies that the income from their вакф is to go toward educating orphans, the person managing it afterward has no right to redirect it elsewhere, even if he personally believes the money would do more good somewhere else. The founder's word holds.

In our time, вакф can take different forms: a property itself, the rent that comes from leasing it out, or a share in a business. There is also the question of a вакф made purely of money — where cash is placed into the вакф, invested, and only the return is spent, while the original sum stays intact. A considerable number of scholars, including within the Ханафи tradition, accept this. But it is not something all scholars agree on fully, and this lesson will not pretend otherwise.

Here is why this matters for what is being built now. Historically, вакф has broken down again and again in the very same place — at the hands of whoever was managing it. Conditions set by the founder were forgotten. Property that was supposed to remain untouched was quietly sold. Income meant for orphans or travellers drifted elsewhere. And a hundred years later, there was no way left to check any of it.

A smart contract, by its very nature, is capable of exactly what вакф has always required: fixing a condition in a way that cannot later be altered, and sending income to its intended purpose automatically, without depending on any one person's honesty. This is not something already running — the contracts have been written but not yet released into full operation. But this particular capacity, and not any fondness for new technology, is the reason it was chosen.

If any detail about how this applies to your own savings or gold needs sorting out — especially where the rulings differ between scholars — that is a matter to raise directly with a tutor or a qualified scholar rather than settle from this lesson alone.
